Attention and Transformers, for programmers

Scaled dot-product attention with its shapes, why we divide by , multi-head attention, sinusoidal positional encoding, the causal mask and the full block with norms and shortcuts. All from scratch in NumPy, forward and backward, checked against F.scaled_dot_product_attention, nn.MultiheadAttention, nn.TransformerEncoderLayer and autograd. A 3,972-parameter Transformer really trained on trip logs, its attention map, the comparison with an LSTM, the parameter count and the quadratic cost. With a worked example: the attention of 3 tokens with , by hand.

Summary

  • Each position computes a query , a key and a value ; the weights mix the values. Cost , a path of length 1 between any two positions and no sequential dependency.
  • Our attention, multi-head attention and block in NumPy match PyTorch to within forward and in the gradients; central differences, to within .
  • A one-block Transformer (, 2 heads) learns to predict the depot after “return” (10–35 tokens back) in 100% of the test trips and the last fault code after “workshop” in 99.2%. Without positional encoding, the last code drops to 62.4%, the same as picking at random among the lit ones (60.7%).
  • An LSTM with 3,780 parameters and the same training gets the nearby code right (98.2%) but not the distant depot: 51.5%, 24.7% and 24.2% with three seeds, against the Transformer's 100% on all three.
tokens→ embedding + position→ block: LN → attention → + → LN → FFN → +→ LN → linear → softmax

§1 · The problem

From a single state to looking directly

A recurrent network summarizes the prefix in a fixed-size state , computed in steps that depend on one another. Two consequences: the information from position reaches position along a path of multiplications (with the vanishing or exploding gradient of topic 9), and training can't be parallelized along the sequence.

Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio (ICLR 2015) added to a recurrent translator a mechanism that, at each output step, computes a weighted average of all the input states, with learned weights. Vaswani et al. (NIPS 2017) removed the recurrence and kept only the attention: the Transformer. It's the architecture of BERT (Devlin et al., NAACL 2019), of the GPT family (Radford et al., 2018 and 2019; Brown et al., NeurIPS 2020) and of almost every current language model.

§2 · Scaled dot-product attention

Queries, keys and values, with their shapes

The sequence is a matrix , one row per token (its embedding from topic 10 plus the position). Three learned linear projections give

and the attention is

is the scaled dot product; each row of is a distribution (the softmax from topic 4), and the output at position is the average of the values weighted by it. is the mask: 0 where looking is allowed and where it isn't, so that . The causal mask is if : each position sees only its past.

Backward, with , the softmax Jacobian applied row by row gives

The masked positions have and therefore gradient 0: the future receives nothing.

atencion.py · attention, multi-head, norm, block and model, forward and backward

"""Attention, multi-head attention and a Transformer block from scratch in NumPy: forward and backward.
Convention: a sequence is a matrix X of shape (n, d), one row per token; the layers are X @ W + b."""
import numpy as np


def softmax(Z):
    Z = Z - Z.max(-1, keepdims=True)                   # subtracting the max changes nothing and avoids overflow
    E = np.exp(Z)
    return E / E.sum(-1, keepdims=True)


def mascara_causal(n):
    return np.triu(np.ones((n, n), dtype=bool), 1)      # True above the diagonal: the future


def atencion(Q, K, V, causal=False):
    """Q, K: (n, dk) · V: (n, dv) → output (n, dv) and weights A (n, n); each row of A adds up to 1."""
    S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(Q.shape[-1])
    if causal:
        S = np.where(mascara_causal(len(S)), -np.inf, S)   # e^−∞ = 0: nobody looks at the future
    A = softmax(S)
    return A @ V, A


def atencion_atras(dO, Q, K, V, A):
    dV = A.T @ dO
    dA = dO @ V.T
    dS = A * (dA - (dA * A).sum(-1, keepdims=True))     # softmax Jacobian, row by row
    dS = dS / np.sqrt(Q.shape[-1])                      # (where the mask put 0, dS is 0 too)
    return dS @ K, dS.T @ Q, dV


def mha(X, P, h, causal=False):
    """Multi-head attention: h heads of size d/h over slices of Q, K and V; they are concatenated and mixed with Wo."""
    Q, K, V = X @ P["Wq"] + P["bq"], X @ P["Wk"] + P["bk"], X @ P["Wv"] + P["bv"]
    dh = Q.shape[1] // h
    sl = [slice(i * dh, (i + 1) * dh) for i in range(h)]
    sal = [atencion(Q[:, s], K[:, s], V[:, s], causal) for s in sl]
    C = np.concatenate([o for o, _ in sal], axis=1)
    cache = (X, Q, K, V, C, [a for _, a in sal], sl)
    return C @ P["Wo"] + P["bo"], cache


def mha_atras(dY, cache, P):
    X, Q, K, V, C, As, sl = cache
    g = {"Wo": C.T @ dY, "bo": dY.sum(0)}
    dC = dY @ P["Wo"].T
    dQ, dK, dV = np.zeros_like(Q), np.zeros_like(K), np.zeros_like(V)
    for s, A in zip(sl, As):
        dQ[:, s], dK[:, s], dV[:, s] = atencion_atras(dC[:, s], Q[:, s], K[:, s], V[:, s], A)
    for n, dZ in (("q", dQ), ("k", dK), ("v", dV)):
        g["W" + n], g["b" + n] = X.T @ dZ, dZ.sum(0)
    return dQ @ P["Wq"].T + dK @ P["Wk"].T + dV @ P["Wv"].T, g


def capa_norma(X, g, b, eps=1e-5):
    mu, var = X.mean(-1, keepdims=True), X.var(-1, keepdims=True)
    Xh = (X - mu) / np.sqrt(var + eps)
    return g * Xh + b, (Xh, np.sqrt(var + eps), g)


def capa_norma_atras(dY, cache):
    Xh, s, g = cache
    dXh = dY * g
    dX = (dXh - dXh.mean(-1, keepdims=True) - Xh * (dXh * Xh).mean(-1, keepdims=True)) / s
    return dX, (dY * Xh).sum(0), dY.sum(0)


def bloque(X, P, h, causal=False):
    """Transformer block with the norm in front (pre-LN), like GPT-2:
    H = X + MHA(LN1(X)) · Y = H + FFN(LN2(H)), with FFN(z) = ReLU(z W1 + b1) W2 + b2 at each position."""
    A, c1 = capa_norma(X, P["g1"], P["be1"])
    M, cm = mha(A, P, h, causal)
    H = X + M                                           # residual connection
    B, c2 = capa_norma(H, P["g2"], P["be2"])
    Z = B @ P["W1"] + P["b1"]
    R = np.maximum(Z, 0)
    Y = H + R @ P["W2"] + P["b2"]                       # another residual connection
    return Y, (c1, cm, c2, B, Z, R)


def bloque_atras(dY, cache, P):
    c1, cm, c2, B, Z, R = cache
    g = {"W2": R.T @ dY, "b2": dY.sum(0)}
    dZ = (dY @ P["W2"].T) * (Z > 0)
    g["W1"], g["b1"] = B.T @ dZ, dZ.sum(0)
    dH, g["g2"], g["be2"] = capa_norma_atras(dZ @ P["W1"].T, c2)
    dH = dH + dY                                        # the shortcut lets the gradient through unchanged
    dA, gm = mha_atras(dH, cm, P)
    g.update(gm)
    dX, g["g1"], g["be1"] = capa_norma_atras(dA, c1)
    return dX + dH, g


def posiciones(n, d):
    """Sinusoidal positional encoding (Vaswani et al., 2017): sine in the even columns, cosine in the odd ones."""
    p = np.arange(n)[:, None]
    w = 1.0 / 10000 ** (np.arange(0, d, 2) / d)
    PE = np.zeros((n, d))
    PE[:, 0::2], PE[:, 1::2] = np.sin(p * w), np.cos(p * w)
    return PE


def modelo(ids, P, h, causal=True):
    """The topic's model: embedding + position → one block → final norm → linear to the vocabulary (logits)."""
    X = P["E"][ids] + posiciones(len(ids), P["E"].shape[1])
    Y, cache = bloque(X, P, h, causal)
    N, cf = capa_norma(Y, P["gf"], P["bef"])
    return N @ P["Wout"] + P["bout"], (ids, cache, cf, N)


def modelo_atras(dZ, cache, P):
    ids, cb, cf, N = cache
    g = {"Wout": N.T @ dZ, "bout": dZ.sum(0)}
    dY, g["gf"], g["bef"] = capa_norma_atras(dZ @ P["Wout"].T, cf)
    dX, gb = bloque_atras(dY, cb, P)
    g.update(gb)
    g["E"] = np.zeros_like(P["E"])
    np.add.at(g["E"], ids, dX)                          # the embedding table from topic 10: sparse gradient
    return g


def entropia_cruzada(Z, y):
    """Mean loss −ln p(y) and its gradient with respect to the logits (softmax − one-hot) / n."""
    P = softmax(Z)
    n = len(y)
    dZ = P.copy()
    dZ[np.arange(n), y] -= 1
    return -np.log(P[np.arange(n), y]).mean(), dZ / n

§3 · The scale factor

Why

If the components of and are independent, with mean 0 and variance 1, then is a sum of terms with mean 0 and variance 1:

Without dividing, the scores spread apart like and the softmax gets close to a one-hot. There, its Jacobian tends to zero and the gradient toward and dies out (Vaswani et al., 2017, §3.2.1).

escala.py · actual output

"""Why we divide by √d: with q and k having independent components of mean 0 and variance 1, q·k is a sum
of d terms of variance 1, so its variance is d. Without dividing, the softmax saturates and its gradient dies."""
import json
import numpy as np
from atencion import softmax

rng = np.random.default_rng(2017)
n, claves = 20000, 10                          # 20,000 questions, each one against 10 keys
print(f"{n} questions q against {claves} keys k, components N(0, 1)")
print("   d   std. dev. of q·k      mean max weight      entropy (max ln 10 = 2.303)     mean |gradient|")
print("                 not divided   not divided / ÷√d   not divided / ÷√d               not divided / ÷√d")
tabla = {}
for d in (2, 8, 16, 64, 128, 512):
    q = rng.normal(size=(n, 1, d)); k = rng.normal(size=(n, claves, d))
    S = (q * k).sum(-1)                        # (n, 10): the scores of each question
    fila = []
    for Z in (S, S / np.sqrt(d)):
        P = softmax(Z)
        H = -(P * np.log(np.maximum(P, 1e-300))).sum(-1)
        J = np.abs(P * (1 - P)).sum(-1)        # size of the diagonal of the softmax Jacobian
        fila.append((P.max(-1).mean(), H.mean(), J.mean()))
    tabla[d] = [round(float(S.std()), 3)] + [round(float(v), 4) for f in fila for v in f]
    print(f"{d:4d}   {S.std():8.2f}  (√d = {np.sqrt(d):5.2f})    {fila[0][0]:.3f} / {fila[1][0]:.3f}"
          f"        {fila[0][1]:.3f} / {fila[1][1]:.3f}                     {fila[0][2]:.3f} / {fila[1][2]:.3f}")
json.dump(tabla, open("escala.json", "w", encoding="utf-8"))
# 20000 questions q against 10 keys k, components N(0, 1)
#    d   std. dev. of q·k      mean max weight      entropy (max ln 10 = 2.303)     mean |gradient|
#                  not divided   not divided / ÷√d   not divided / ÷√d               not divided / ÷√d
#    2       1.42  (√d =  1.41)    0.368 / 0.290        1.770 / 1.971                     0.750 / 0.814
#    8       2.83  (√d =  2.83)    0.620 / 0.312        1.067 / 1.937                     0.506 / 0.807
#   16       3.98  (√d =  4.00)    0.724 / 0.314        0.752 / 1.934                     0.378 / 0.807
#   64       8.00  (√d =  8.00)    0.862 / 0.318        0.353 / 1.927                     0.194 / 0.806
#  128      11.32  (√d = 11.31)    0.906 / 0.321        0.238 / 1.922                     0.135 / 0.804
#  512      22.63  (√d = 22.63)    0.953 / 0.320        0.115 / 1.924                     0.068 / 0.805

The measured standard deviation follows in every case (22.63 with ). Without dividing, with (the head size of the base Transformer) the favorite key takes 86.2% of the weight on average, and the sum , which measures how much the softmax can change, drops from 0.81 to 0.19; with 512, to 0.07. Dividing, everything stays where it was with : maximum weight around 32% and entropy of 1.92–1.97 out of a maximum of . In the toy of the simple version, the temperature slider also divides by : .

§4 · Multi-head, position and mask

Several attentions at once, and the order added in

With heads, : each head uses its own slice of the columns of , and , and the outputs are concatenated and mixed with :

The cost is that of a single head of size , but each head has its own pattern . The PyTorch format. nn.MultiheadAttention stores the three projections stacked in in_proj_weight, of shape : rows are , rows , , and rows , (transposed because nn.Linear computes ). The biases go the same way in in_proj_bias, and in out_proj.weight. The heads don't have separate matrices: head is columns of the result.

Position. Attention is permutation-equivariant: if the rows of are permuted, the output is permuted the same way. Without information about order, from a given position the rest of the sequence is a set. The sinusoidal encoding adds to row

with wavelengths from to . For each frequency, is a rotation of that depends only on , so a dot product can express relative offsets. The learned alternatives (a table of positions, as in GPT-2) or relative ones work similarly; the sinusoidal one has no parameters.

Causal mask. With it, the output at position depends only on . That way you can train to predict the next token at every position of a sequence in a single parallel pass (teacher forcing), and then generate token by token. BERT uses attention without a mask and learns to fill in gaps; GPT, with a mask, learns to continue.

§5 · The block

Attention, per-position network, shortcuts and norms

We use the variant with the norm in front (pre-LN), the one in GPT-2, which is more stable to train than the original with the norm after:

  • Shortcuts. The residual connections of He et al. (CVPR 2016): includes the identity, so the gradient goes through many blocks without vanishing.
  • Norms. LayerNorm (Ba, Kiros and Hinton, 2016) normalizes each row over its components, not over the batch like the batch norm of topic 7: it doesn't depend on the batch size or on the length.
  • FFN. A two-layer network (topic 3), typically , applied to each position separately with the same weights. Attention mixes across positions; the FFN transforms each one.
  • Dropout (topic 7) is applied to the attention weights and to the output of each sublayer during training; here, with a tiny model, we don't use it.

check.py · against PyTorch 2.15 (CPU, float64)

"""Check of atencion.py against PyTorch (float64): F.scaled_dot_product_attention, nn.MultiheadAttention,
nn.TransformerEncoderLayer, autograd and central differences; and the trained model, evaluated with NumPy only."""
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch import nn
import atencion as A
from datos import datos
from modelo import Viajero, a_numpy, perdida

torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
n, d, h = 9, 16, 2
t = lambda x: torch.tensor(x, requires_grad=True)
err = lambda a, b: float(np.max(np.abs(np.asarray(a) - (b.detach().numpy() if torch.is_tensor(b) else b))))
print(f"PyTorch {torch.__version__} · sequence of {n} tokens, d = {d}, {h} heads · maximum absolute error")

# 1. single-head attention
Q, K, Vm, dO = (rng.normal(size=(n, 8)) for _ in range(4))
for causal in (False, True):
    O, W = A.atencion(Q, K, Vm, causal)
    q, k, v = t(Q), t(K), t(Vm)
    o = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=causal); o.backward(torch.tensor(dO))
    dq, dk, dv = A.atencion_atras(dO, Q, K, Vm, W)
    print(f"  scaled_dot_product_attention{' causal' if causal else '       '}  output {err(O, o):.1e}"
          f"   dQ {err(dq, q.grad):.1e}  dK {err(dk, k.grad):.1e}  dV {err(dv, v.grad):.1e}")

# 2. multi-head: nn.MultiheadAttention stores Wq, Wk and Wv stacked in in_proj_weight (3d × d), each one transposed
P = {f"W{c}": rng.normal(0, 0.3, (d, d)) for c in "qkvo"} | {f"b{c}": rng.normal(0, 0.1, d) for c in "qkvo"}
X = rng.normal(size=(n, d))
mha = nn.MultiheadAttention(d, h, batch_first=True)
with torch.no_grad():
    mha.in_proj_weight.copy_(torch.tensor(np.concatenate([P["Wq"].T, P["Wk"].T, P["Wv"].T])))
    mha.in_proj_bias.copy_(torch.tensor(np.concatenate([P["bq"], P["bk"], P["bv"]])))
    mha.out_proj.weight.copy_(torch.tensor(P["Wo"].T)); mha.out_proj.bias.copy_(torch.tensor(P["bo"]))
Y, cache = A.mha(X, P, h, causal=True)
y, w = mha(*(torch.tensor(X[None]),) * 3, attn_mask=torch.tensor(A.mascara_causal(n)), average_attn_weights=False)
print(f"  nn.MultiheadAttention causal        output {err(Y, y[0]):.1e}   weights of the 2 heads {err(np.stack(cache[5]), w[0]):.1e}")

# 3. the full block against nn.TransformerEncoderLayer (norm in front, no dropout) and its autograd
P |= {"g1": 1 + rng.normal(0, 0.1, d), "be1": rng.normal(0, 0.1, d), "g2": 1 + rng.normal(0, 0.1, d),
      "be2": rng.normal(0, 0.1, d), "W1": rng.normal(0, 0.3, (d, 4 * d)), "b1": rng.normal(0, 0.1, 4 * d),
      "W2": rng.normal(0, 0.3, (4 * d, d)), "b2": rng.normal(0, 0.1, d)}
capa = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d, h, dim_feedforward=4 * d, dropout=0.0, batch_first=True, norm_first=True)
with torch.no_grad():
    capa.self_attn.in_proj_weight.copy_(mha.in_proj_weight); capa.self_attn.in_proj_bias.copy_(mha.in_proj_bias)
    capa.self_attn.out_proj.weight.copy_(mha.out_proj.weight); capa.self_attn.out_proj.bias.copy_(mha.out_proj.bias)
    for lin, W, b in ((capa.linear1, "W1", "b1"), (capa.linear2, "W2", "b2")):
        lin.weight.copy_(torch.tensor(P[W].T)); lin.bias.copy_(torch.tensor(P[b]))
    for ln, g, b in ((capa.norm1, "g1", "be1"), (capa.norm2, "g2", "be2")):
        ln.weight.copy_(torch.tensor(P[g])); ln.bias.copy_(torch.tensor(P[b]))
dY = rng.normal(size=(n, d))
Yb, cb = A.bloque(X, P, h, causal=True)
x = t(X[None])
yb = capa(x, src_mask=nn.Transformer.generate_square_subsequent_mask(n), is_causal=True); yb.backward(torch.tensor(dY[None]))
dX, g = A.bloque_atras(dY, cb, P)
ref = {"Wq": capa.self_attn.in_proj_weight.grad[:d].T, "Wk": capa.self_attn.in_proj_weight.grad[d:2 * d].T,
       "Wv": capa.self_attn.in_proj_weight.grad[2 * d:].T, "Wo": capa.self_attn.out_proj.weight.grad.T,
       "W1": capa.linear1.weight.grad.T, "W2": capa.linear2.weight.grad.T, "g1": capa.norm1.weight.grad, "g2": capa.norm2.weight.grad}
print(f"  nn.TransformerEncoderLayer causal   output {err(Yb, yb[0]):.1e}   dX {err(dX, x.grad[0]):.1e}"
      f"   weights {max(err(g[k], v) for k, v in ref.items()):.1e}")

# 4. central differences over the block: L = sum(Y · dY)
def L_(Pp, Xp):
    return float((A.bloque(Xp, Pp, h, True)[0] * dY).sum())
eps, peor = 1e-6, 0.0
for k in ("Wq", "Wk", "W1", "g2"):
    for idx in [tuple(rng.integers(0, s) for s in P[k].shape) for _ in range(5)]:
        Pm, Pp = {a: b.copy() for a, b in P.items()}, {a: b.copy() for a, b in P.items()}
        Pp[k][idx] += eps; Pm[k][idx] -= eps
        peor = max(peor, abs((L_(Pp, X) - L_(Pm, X)) / (2 * eps) - g[k][idx]))
print(f"  central differences (20 weights)     gradient {peor:.1e}")

# 5. the trained model (viajero.pt), evaluated with NumPy on the 1,000 test trips
m = Viajero(); m.load_state_dict(torch.load("viajero.pt")); Pm = a_numpy(m)
Xt, Lt = datos()[2]
tot, cnt, e_logit = 0.0, 0, 0.0
with torch.no_grad():
    Zt = m(torch.tensor(Xt)).numpy()
    lt = perdida(torch.tensor(Zt), torch.tensor(Xt), torch.tensor(Lt)).item()
for i in range(len(Xt)):
    ids = Xt[i, :Lt[i]]
    Z, _ = A.modelo(ids, Pm, 2)
    e_logit = max(e_logit, np.max(np.abs(Z - Zt[i, :Lt[i]])))
    l, _ = A.entropia_cruzada(Z[:-1], ids[1:]); tot += l * (len(ids) - 1); cnt += len(ids) - 1
print(f"  trained model, 1,000 trips          logits {e_logit:.1e}   loss NumPy {tot / cnt:.6f} · PyTorch {lt:.6f}")
ids = Xt[0, :Lt[0]]
Z, cm = A.modelo(ids, Pm, 2)
_, dZ = A.entropia_cruzada(Z[:-1], ids[1:])
gm = A.modelo_atras(np.vstack([dZ, np.zeros((1, Z.shape[1]))]), cm, Pm)
m.zero_grad(); F.cross_entropy(m(torch.tensor(ids[None]))[0, :-1], torch.tensor(ids[1:])).backward()
tg = {"E": m.E.weight.grad, "Wq": m.q.weight.grad.T, "W1": m.f1.weight.grad.T, "Wout": m.sal.weight.grad.T, "gf": m.lnf.weight.grad}
print(f"  model gradients, one trip           {max(err(gm[k], v) for k, v in tg.items()):.1e}"
      f"   (rows of E with a gradient: {int((np.abs(gm['E']).sum(1) > 0).sum())} of 20)")

Everything matches to the last bit or nearly so: attention with and without the mask, its three gradients, multi-head attention with the weights copied into the stacked format and the full block against nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(norm_first=True, dropout=0), with the gradients of the input and of all the weights. The central differences have the expected truncation error with . The trained model from §6, evaluated with atencion.py only, gives the same loss on the 1,000 test trips, and its gradients match autograd; of the embedding table, only the 13 rows of the tokens that appear in that trip get a gradient.

§6 · The experiment

A tiny Transformer that reads trip logs

Each trip is a sequence of 14 to 39 tokens from a vocabulary of 20: “departure”, the depot (4), 6 to 26 events (8 types, at random) among which 1 to 3 different fault codes turn on (the ones from topic 10), “workshop” followed by the last code that turned on, 1 to 6 more events, “return”, the departure depot and “end”. The task is a language model's: cross-entropy of the next token at each position, with a causal mask. Two tokens per trip are deterministic and measure what it has learned: the depot after “return”, 10–35 positions away from its copy, and the code after “workshop”, which requires knowing which of the lit ones is the last.

datos.py · the trips

"""Data for topic 11: the log of a trip, as a sequence of tokens. The truck's black box writes down what
happens: it leaves a depot, loads, unloads, brakes, gets stuck in traffic… Sometimes a fault code turns on
(the ones from topic 10). At the end it stops at the workshop, where the mechanic writes down the LAST code
that turned on, and it returns to the depot it left from.

The task is a language model's: predict the next token. Almost all of them are unpredictable (the trip's
events are random), but two can always be guessed right by looking back carefully:
  · after "return" comes the departure depot, which is at the start, far back;
  · after "workshop" comes the last fault code that turned on, which may not be the only one."""
import numpy as np

ESPECIALES = ["departure", "return", "workshop", "end"]
DEPOSITOS = ["Madrid", "Zaragoza", "Valencia", "Sevilla"]
CODIGOS = ["P0217", "P0299", "C0035", "P0562"]          # overheating, turbo, wheel sensor, low voltage
SUCESOS = ["loading", "unloading", "idling", "braking", "traffic", "refueling", "toll", "stop"]
VOCAB = ESPECIALES + DEPOSITOS + CODIGOS + SUCESOS
V = len(VOCAB)                                         # 20 tokens
ID = {t: i for i, t in enumerate(VOCAB)}
TMAX = 40                                              # the longest possible trip


def viaje(rng):
    """departure D · 6–26 events with 1–3 different codes among them · workshop C · 1–6 events · return D · end"""
    d = DEPOSITOS[rng.integers(4)]
    n1 = rng.integers(6, 27)
    medio = [SUCESOS[k] for k in rng.integers(0, 8, n1)]
    nc = rng.integers(1, 4)
    cods = [CODIGOS[k] for k in rng.choice(4, nc, replace=False)]
    for c, p in zip(cods, np.sort(rng.choice(n1, nc, replace=False))):
        medio[p] = c                                    # the codes replace events, in order of appearance
    n2 = rng.integers(1, 7)
    cola = [SUCESOS[k] for k in rng.integers(0, 8, n2)]
    return ["departure", d] + medio + ["workshop", cods[-1]] + cola + ["return", d, "end"]


def conjunto(n, seed):
    """n trips as a matrix of indices (n, TMAX), padded with "end", and their lengths."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    vs = [viaje(rng) for _ in range(n)]
    X = np.full((n, TMAX), ID["end"], dtype=np.int64)
    L = np.array([len(v) for v in vs])
    for i, v in enumerate(vs):
        X[i, :len(v)] = [ID[t] for t in v]
    return X, L


def datos():
    """Training (2,000 trips), validation (500) and test (1,000), with fixed seeds."""
    return conjunto(2000, 11), conjunto(500, 111), conjunto(1000, 1111)


def clave(X, L):
    """The positions that can be guessed right: the token after "return" and the one after "workshop".
    Returns two lists of (trip, position of the question) and the distance to the hidden answer."""
    reg, tal = [], []
    for i in range(len(X)):
        v = X[i, :L[i]].tolist()
        reg.append((i, v.index(ID["return"]), v.index(ID["return"]) - 1))        # distance to the depot (pos. 1)
        t = v.index(ID["workshop"]); ult = max(p for p in range(t) if VOCAB[v[p]] in CODIGOS)
        tal.append((i, t, t - ult))
    return reg, tal


if __name__ == "__main__":
    (X, L), (Xv, Lv), (Xt, Lt) = datos()
    print(f"vocabulary: {V} tokens · trips of {L.min()} to {L.max()} tokens (mean {L.mean():.1f})")
    print("example:", " ".join(VOCAB[k] for k in X[0, :L[0]]))
    reg, tal = clave(Xt, Lt)
    dr = np.array([r[2] for r in reg]); dt = np.array([t[2] for t in tal])
    nc = np.array([sum(VOCAB[k] in CODIGOS for k in Xt[i, :Lt[i]]) - 1 for i in range(len(Xt))])
    print(f"test: depot {dr.min()}–{dr.max()} tokens before \"return\" (mean {dr.mean():.1f});"
          f" last code {dt.min()}–{dt.max()} before \"workshop\" (mean {dt.mean():.1f})")
    print(f"trips with 1, 2 and 3 codes: {[int((nc == k).sum()) for k in (1, 2, 3)]}")
    print(f"accuracy guessing at random: depot {1/4:.0%}, code {1/4:.0%};"
          f" picking a lit code at random: {np.mean(1 / nc):.1%}")
# vocabulary: 20 tokens · trips of 14 to 39 tokens (mean 26.5)
# example: departure Madrid toll P0562 traffic C0035 refueling loading braking unloading workshop C0035 stop traffic toll idling unloading traffic return Madrid end
# test: depot 10–35 tokens before "return" (mean 22.6); last code 1–24 before "workshop" (mean 6.2)
# trips with 1, 2 and 3 codes: [332, 316, 352]
# accuracy guessing at random: depot 25%, code 25%; picking a lit code at random: 60.7%

modelo.py · the model in PyTorch, the LSTM for comparison and the training

"""The topic's tiny Transformer in PyTorch (the same math as atencion.py) and its training:
predict the next token of the trip log, with a causal mask, Adam with warm-up and fixed seeds."""
import time
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch import nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from datos import V, TMAX

torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)


def posiciones(n, d):
    p = torch.arange(n)[:, None].double()
    w = 1.0 / 10000 ** (torch.arange(0, d, 2).double() / d)
    PE = torch.zeros(n, d)
    PE[:, 0::2], PE[:, 1::2] = torch.sin(p * w), torch.cos(p * w)
    return PE


class Lectora(nn.Module):
    """The alternative from topic 9: embedding (V×d) → LSTM with H units, token by token → linear H→V.
    As in topic 9, the forget gate starts almost open (bias 3) so the memory lasts."""
    def __init__(s, d=16, H=20, sesgo_olvido=3.0):
        super().__init__()
        s.E, s.rec, s.sal = nn.Embedding(V, d), nn.LSTM(d, H, batch_first=True), nn.Linear(H, V)
        with torch.no_grad():
            s.rec.bias_ih_l0[H:2 * H] = sesgo_olvido; s.rec.bias_hh_l0[H:2 * H] = 0.0

    def forward(s, ids, causal=True):
        return s.sal(s.rec(s.E(ids))[0])


class Viajero(nn.Module):
    """embedding (V×d) + position → LN → attention with h heads → residual → LN → FFN d→4d→d → residual → LN → d→V"""
    def __init__(s, d=16, h=2, con_posicion=True):
        super().__init__()
        s.d, s.h, s.con_posicion = d, h, con_posicion
        s.E = nn.Embedding(V, d)
        s.ln1, s.ln2, s.lnf = nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.LayerNorm(d)
        s.q, s.k, s.v, s.o = (nn.Linear(d, d) for _ in range(4))
        s.f1, s.f2 = nn.Linear(d, 4 * d), nn.Linear(4 * d, d)
        s.sal = nn.Linear(d, V)
        s.register_buffer("PE", posiciones(TMAX, d))

    def forward(s, ids, causal=True, pesos=False):
        n, T = ids.shape
        X = s.E(ids) + (s.PE[:T] if s.con_posicion else 0)
        A = s.ln1(X)
        dh = s.d // s.h
        sep = lambda Z: Z.view(n, T, s.h, dh).transpose(1, 2)          # (n, h, T, dh)
        Q, K, Vv = sep(s.q(A)), sep(s.k(A)), sep(s.v(A))
        S = Q @ K.transpose(-1, -2) / dh ** 0.5
        if causal:
            S = S.masked_fill(torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, dtype=torch.bool), 1), float("-inf"))
        W = S.softmax(-1)
        H = X + s.o((W @ Vv).transpose(1, 2).reshape(n, T, s.d))
        Y = H + s.f2(F.relu(s.f1(s.ln2(H))))
        Z = s.sal(s.lnf(Y))
        return (Z, W) if pesos else Z


def n_param(m):
    return sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())


def a_numpy(m):
    """The model's weights with the convention of atencion.py (X @ W: the nn.Linear ones are transposed)."""
    t = lambda x: x.detach().numpy().copy()
    P = {"E": t(m.E.weight), "Wout": t(m.sal.weight).T, "bout": t(m.sal.bias)}
    for n, lin in (("q", m.q), ("k", m.k), ("v", m.v), ("o", m.o)):
        P["W" + n], P["b" + n] = t(lin.weight).T, t(lin.bias)
    P["W1"], P["b1"], P["W2"], P["b2"] = t(m.f1.weight).T, t(m.f1.bias), t(m.f2.weight).T, t(m.f2.bias)
    for n, ln in (("1", m.ln1), ("2", m.ln2), ("f", m.lnf)):
        P["g" + n], P["be" + n] = t(ln.weight), t(ln.bias)
    return P


def perdida(Z, X, L):
    """Cross-entropy of predicting X[:, t+1] from position t, only inside each trip."""
    T = X.shape[1]
    dentro = torch.arange(T - 1)[None, :] < (L[:, None] - 1)
    return F.cross_entropy(Z[:, :-1][dentro], X[:, 1:][dentro])


def entrenar(X, L, Xv, Lv, d=16, h=2, con_posicion=True, epocas=100, lr=3e-3, calentamiento=200, lote=32, seed=0, crear=None):
    """Adam with a linear warm-up of the learning rate (topic 6) during the first steps.
    Returns the model, the validation loss per epoch and the seconds it took."""
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    m = crear() if crear else Viajero(d, h, con_posicion)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(m.parameters(), lr=lr)
    sched = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.LambdaLR(opt, lambda paso: min(1.0, (paso + 1) / calentamiento))
    X, L, Xv, Lv = (torch.tensor(a) for a in (X, L, Xv, Lv))
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed + 1)
    curva, t0 = [], time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(epocas):
        orden = torch.randperm(len(X), generator=g)
        for k in range(0, len(X), lote):
            j = orden[k:k + lote]
            opt.zero_grad(); perdida(m(X[j]), X[j], L[j]).backward(); opt.step(); sched.step()
        with torch.no_grad():
            curva.append(perdida(m(Xv), Xv, Lv).item())
    return m, curva, time.perf_counter() - t0


def aciertos(pred, X, preguntas):
    """Fraction of questions (trip, position) where the most likely token is the real next one."""
    return float(np.mean([pred[i, t] == X[i, t + 1] for i, t, _ in preguntas]))

entrenar.py · actual output

"""Trains the topic's tiny Transformer (d = 16, 2 heads, one block) and two variants:
without positional encoding and with a single head. Measures the accuracy on the two questions that can be
guessed right and where attention looks from "return" and from "workshop". Saves the main one in viajero.pt
and the one that knows nothing about positions in viajero_sin_posicion.pt."""
import numpy as np
import torch
from datos import datos, clave, VOCAB, CODIGOS, DEPOSITOS
from modelo import entrenar, n_param, aciertos

(X, L), (Xv, Lv), (Xt, Lt) = datos()
reg, tal = clave(Xt, Lt)


def mide(m):
    with torch.no_grad():
        Z, W = m(torch.tensor(Xt), pesos=True)
    pred, W = Z.argmax(-1).numpy(), W.numpy()                       # W: (trips, heads, T, T)
    # weight each head puts, from the question, on the token that hides the answer
    a_dep = W[[i for i, _, _ in reg], :, [t for _, t, _ in reg], 1].mean(0)
    a_cod = W[[i for i, _, _ in tal], :, [t for _, t, _ in tal], [t - dd for _, t, dd in tal]].mean(0)
    return aciertos(pred, Xt, reg), aciertos(pred, Xt, tal), a_dep, a_cod


resultados = {}
for nombre, kw in [("main: 2 heads, with position", {}), ("without positional encoding", {"con_posicion": False}),
                   ("a single head", {"h": 1})]:
    m, curva, seg = entrenar(X, L, Xv, Lv, **kw)
    ad, ac, wd, wc = mide(m)
    print(f"{nombre} · {n_param(m)} parameters")
    print(f"  validation loss at epoch 1, 10, 25, 50, 100: {', '.join(f'{curva[e - 1]:.3f}' for e in (1, 10, 25, 50, 100))}")
    print(f"  accuracy on 1,000 test trips: depot after \"return\" {ad:.1%} · last code after \"workshop\" {ac:.1%}")
    print(f"  mean weight of each head on the key token: depot {np.round(wd, 3).tolist()} · code {np.round(wc, 3).tolist()}")
    if len(resultados) < 2:
        torch.save(m.state_dict(), "viajero.pt" if not resultados else "viajero_sin_posicion.pt")
    resultados[nombre] = (ad, ac)
# main: 2 heads, with position · 3972 parameters
#   validation loss at epoch 1, 10, 25, 50, 100: 2.868, 2.062, 2.017, 2.017, 2.015
#   accuracy on 1,000 test trips: depot after "return" 100.0% · last code after "workshop" 99.2%
#   mean weight of each head on the key token: depot [0.656, 0.561] · code [0.886, 0.054]
# without positional encoding · 3972 parameters
#   validation loss at epoch 1, 10, 25, 50, 100: 2.866, 2.071, 2.051, 2.044, 2.046
#   accuracy on 1,000 test trips: depot after "return" 100.0% · last code after "workshop" 62.4%
#   mean weight of each head on the key token: depot [0.002, 0.728] · code [0.404, 0.299]
# a single head · 3972 parameters
#   validation loss at epoch 1, 10, 25, 50, 100: 2.868, 2.069, 2.023, 2.017, 2.013
#   accuracy on 1,000 test trips: depot after "return" 100.0% · last code after "workshop" 99.6%
#   mean weight of each head on the key token: depot [0.729] · code [0.878]

The main model (, 2 heads of 8, one block, FFN of 64) gets the depot right in all 1,000 trips and the last code in 99.2%. The validation loss goes down to 2.015; a good part of it is irreducible, because the events are random ( nats per event). The heads split the work: from “workshop”, head 1 puts on average 88.6% of its attention on the last code and head 2 only 5.4%; from “return”, both look at the depot (65.6% and 56.1%). Without positional encoding, the depot is still right (it's the only token of its type before “return”, order isn't needed), but the last code drops to 62.4%: from “workshop”, the lit codes are an unordered set. A single head of 16 is enough for this task (99.6%).

Head

Causal mask

0.254

The widget runs the trained model in the browser (the weights of viajero.pt, rounded to 5 decimals: the probabilities change by at most ) on trip 374 of the test set. Tap a row to see its weights and the prediction. With , from “return” the heads put 90.5% and 88.3% on “Valencia” and the model gives 99.7% to Valencia; with the weights drop to 23.3% and 33.3% and the model gets it wrong (Zaragoza, 92.9%). Without the mask, the model sees positions it never saw during training and its output stops making sense: from “workshop” it predicts P0562, a code that isn't in the trip.

§7 · Against the LSTM

The same task, with recurrent memory

The LSTM from topic 9 (embedding of 16, 20 units, initial forget bias 3, 3,780 parameters) with the same training: 100 epochs, Adam with linear warm-up over 200 steps and batches of 32 (topic 6), three seeds.

comparar.py · actual output

"""The tiny Transformer against an LSTM from topic 9 with a similar number of parameters, on the same task
and with the same training (100 epochs, Adam with warm-up), with three seeds."""
import json
import numpy as np
import torch
from datos import datos, clave
from modelo import entrenar, n_param, aciertos, Lectora

(X, L), (Xv, Lv), (Xt, Lt) = datos()
reg, tal = clave(Xt, Lt)
TRAMOS = [(1, 2), (3, 5), (6, 10), (11, 24)]                       # distance to the last code
TRAMOS_D = [(10, 17), (18, 24), (25, 35)]                          # distance to the depot


def mide(m):
    with torch.no_grad():
        pred = m(torch.tensor(Xt)).argmax(-1).numpy()
    porTramo = [aciertos(pred, Xt, [q for q in tal if a <= q[2] <= b]) for a, b in TRAMOS]
    porTramoD = [aciertos(pred, Xt, [q for q in reg if a <= q[2] <= b]) for a, b in TRAMOS_D]
    return aciertos(pred, Xt, reg), aciertos(pred, Xt, tal), porTramo, porTramoD


res = {}
for nombre, crear in [("Transformer", None), ("LSTM", lambda: Lectora(16, 20))]:
    filas = []
    for seed in (0, 1, 2):
        m, curva, seg = entrenar(X, L, Xv, Lv, seed=seed, crear=crear)
        ad, ac, pt, pd = mide(m)
        filas.append((ad, ac, pt, curva, seg, pd))
        print(f"{nombre:11s} seed {seed} · {n_param(m)} parameters · {seg:3.0f} s\n  depot {ad:6.1%} (by distance"
              f" {' '.join(f'{x:.1%}' for x in pd)}) · last code {ac:6.1%} (by distance {' '.join(f'{x:.1%}' for x in pt)})")
    res[nombre] = filas
print("distances to the depot:", ", ".join(f"{a}–{b} ({sum(a <= q[2] <= b for q in reg)} trips)" for a, b in TRAMOS_D))
print("distances to the last code:", ", ".join(f"{a}–{b} ({sum(a <= q[2] <= b for q in tal)} trips)" for a, b in TRAMOS))
for nombre, filas in res.items():
    c = np.array([f[3] for f in filas]).mean(0)
    print(f"{nombre:11s} mean validation loss, epochs 5, 25, 50, 100: {c[4]:.3f} {c[24]:.3f} {c[49]:.3f} {c[99]:.3f}")
json.dump({k: {"dep": [f[0] for f in v], "cod": [f[1] for f in v], "tramos": [f[2] for f in v], "tramos_d": [f[5] for f in v], "seg": [f[4] for f in v],
               "curva": np.array([f[3] for f in v]).mean(0).round(4).tolist()} for k, v in res.items()},
          open("comparar.json", "w", encoding="utf-8"))
# Transformer seed 0 · 3972 parameters ·  47 s
#   depot 100.0% (by distance 100.0% 100.0% 100.0%) · last code  99.2% (by distance 99.3% 100.0% 98.9% 98.3%)
# Transformer seed 1 · 3972 parameters ·  42 s
#   depot 100.0% (by distance 100.0% 100.0% 100.0%) · last code  83.2% (by distance 79.2% 83.9% 83.5% 87.6%)
# Transformer seed 2 · 3972 parameters ·  53 s
#   depot 100.0% (by distance 100.0% 100.0% 100.0%) · last code  97.5% (by distance 96.3% 98.6% 98.5% 96.1%)
# LSTM        seed 0 · 3780 parameters · 135 s
#   depot  51.5% (by distance 52.9% 53.5% 49.0%) · last code  98.2% (by distance 97.4% 98.2% 98.9% 98.3%)
# LSTM        seed 1 · 3780 parameters ·  72 s
#   depot  24.7% (by distance 23.2% 25.8% 24.8%) · last code  83.3% (by distance 90.0% 84.3% 81.0% 75.3%)
# LSTM        seed 2 · 3780 parameters ·  58 s
#   depot  24.2% (by distance 23.6% 25.5% 23.5%) · last code  85.8% (by distance 82.2% 83.2% 90.5% 88.2%)
# distances to the depot: 10–17 (263 trips), 18–24 (325 trips), 25–35 (412 trips)
# distances to the last code: 1–2 (269 trips), 3–5 (280 trips), 6–10 (273 trips), 11–24 (178 trips)
# Transformer mean validation loss, epochs 5, 25, 50, 100: 2.154 2.033 2.019 2.020
# LSTM        mean validation loss, epochs 5, 25, 50, 100: 2.197 2.125 2.107 2.068

The LSTM learns the code, which is 6 positions back on average (98.2% with seed 0), but not the depot: with seed 0 it reaches 51.5%, and with the other two it stays at chance (25%), with no clear differences by distance. The Transformer gets the depot right 100% of the time with all three seeds: to attention, 10 or 35 positions away are the same single step. It isn't that the LSTM can't do it, in topic 9 it remembered a hard brake for 100 readings, but here it has to keep the depot in its state for 10–35 steps while handling a noisy prediction task at each of them, and the signal that rewards it shows up once per trip. The Transformer also depends on the seed: the last code is right 99.2%, 83.2% and 97.5% of the time. And the time per training run, on this CPU, was 42–53 s versus 58–135 s.

§8 · Parameters and cost

How much a block weighs and how much a sequence costs

With the model dimension and that of the FFN, a block has

parameters, independent of and of the length . With , about : two thirds in the FFN.

parametros.py · actual output

"""How many parameters a Transformer block has, checked with nn.TransformerEncoderLayer, and how much memory
the attention matrix takes depending on the sequence length (the quadratic cost)."""
import torch
from torch import nn
from modelo import Viajero, n_param


def bloque(d, f):
    """attention: Wq, Wk, Wv, Wo (d×d) with their biases · FFN d→f→d with biases · two norms (γ and β)"""
    return 4 * (d * d + d), d * f + f + f * d + d, 2 * 2 * d


print("parameters of one block (attention + FFN + norms) · formula and nn.TransformerEncoderLayer")
for nombre, d, h, f in [("this topic", 16, 2, 64), ("base Transformer (2017)", 512, 8, 2048), ("GPT-2 small", 768, 12, 3072)]:
    a, ff, ln = bloque(d, f)
    capa = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(d, h, dim_feedforward=f, batch_first=True)
    print(f"  {nombre:24s} d={d:3d} h={h:2d} FFN {f:4d}: attention {a:9,} + FFN {ff:9,} + norms {ln:5,} = {a + ff + ln:9,}"
          f" · PyTorch {n_param(capa):9,}")
m = Viajero()
partes = {"embedding 20×16": m.E, "block": [m.ln1, m.q, m.k, m.v, m.o, m.ln2, m.f1, m.f2], "final norm": m.lnf, "output 16→20": m.sal}
print("the topic's model:", ", ".join(f"{k} {sum(n_param(x) for x in (v if isinstance(v, list) else [v]))}" for k, v in partes.items()),
      f"= {n_param(m)} (the position is fixed: it isn't learned)")
a, ff, ln = bloque(768, 3072)
gpt2 = 12 * (a + ff + ln) + 50257 * 768 + 1024 * 768 + 2 * 768
print(f"GPT-2 small: 12 blocks {12 * (a + ff + ln):,} + tokens 50,257×768 {50257 * 768:,} + positions 1,024×768"
      f" {1024 * 768:,} + final norm 1,536 = {gpt2:,}")
print("n×n attention matrix of one head in one layer (2 bytes per number):")
for n in (40, 1024, 8192, 131072):
    b = 2 * n * n
    print(f"  n = {n:7,}: {n * n:15,} weights · {b / 2**20:12,.3f} MiB")
# parameters of one block (attention + FFN + norms) · formula and nn.TransformerEncoderLayer
#   this topic               d= 16 h= 2 FFN   64: attention     1,088 + FFN     2,128 + norms    64 =     3,280 · PyTorch     3,280
#   base Transformer (2017)  d=512 h= 8 FFN 2048: attention 1,050,624 + FFN 2,099,712 + norms 2,048 = 3,152,384 · PyTorch 3,152,384
#   GPT-2 small              d=768 h=12 FFN 3072: attention 2,362,368 + FFN 4,722,432 + norms 3,072 = 7,087,872 · PyTorch 7,087,872
# the topic's model: embedding 20×16 320, block 3280, final norm 32, output 16→20 340 = 3972 (the position is fixed: it isn't learned)
# GPT-2 small: 12 blocks 85,054,464 + tokens 50,257×768 38,597,376 + positions 1,024×768 786,432 + final norm 1,536 = 124,439,808
# n×n attention matrix of one head in one layer (2 bytes per number):
#   n =      40:           1,600 weights ·        0.003 MiB
#   n =   1,024:       1,048,576 weights ·        2.000 MiB
#   n =   8,192:      67,108,864 weights ·      128.000 MiB
#   n = 131,072:  17,179,869,184 weights ·   32,768.000 MiB

The formula matches PyTorch in all three cases, and adding the token table and the position table gives exactly the published size of GPT-2 small, 124,439,808 (the output layer shares its weights with the token table). The cost per layer, from table 1 of Vaswani et al. (2017), with an extra column for memory:

LayerOperations per layerSequential operationsMaximum path between positionsExtra memory
Attention per head
Recurrent
Convolution (kernel )

Attention is cheaper than recurrence as long as , and above all it's parallel. The problem shows up with long sequences: the matrix of one head takes 2 MiB with 1,024 positions and 32 GiB with 131,072. Today's implementations (FlashAttention, which scaled_dot_product_attention uses when it can) compute the same in blocks without storing the whole , which reduces the memory but not the operations. When generating, each new token only needs its row of , and the earlier and are stored (the KV cache).

§9 · From the block to the LLM

What a language model is, and what it isn't

  • The recipe. Tokens (pieces of words), embedding and position, causal blocks, a norm and a linear layer to the vocabulary. It's trained exactly like the model in §6: cross-entropy of the next token at each position. GPT-2 small has 12 blocks and ; GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020), 96 blocks, and 175 billion parameters.
  • Generating. A token is sampled from (another temperature, now over the vocabulary), added, and the process repeats. With , always the most likely one.
  • What it doesn't do. There's no database and no checking: it produces likely continuations according to its training data. It can state false things with confidence. Chat assistants add more training (with example conversations and human preferences), but the mechanism is this one.
  • Training. Adam (or AdamW) with learning-rate warm-up, which the original Transformer already used: at the start, Adam's moment estimates are noisy and the attention gradients are large.

§10 · Checklist

Before using attention on your sequences

  • Divide by (or use scaled_dot_product_attention, which already does it) and check that the initial scores have a variance close to 1.
  • Add position information if order matters: without it, attention sees sets.
  • To predict the future, use a causal mask in training and in evaluation; if you pad sequences, mask the padding positions too.
  • If you copy weights into nn.MultiheadAttention, remember the stacking in in_proj_weight.
  • Use learning-rate warm-up and try several seeds: the same model gave 99.2%, 83.2% and 97.5%.
  • Measure the cost with your real lengths: dominates from a few thousand positions on. For long sensor series, chop or summarize first.
  • Don't take an attention map as the complete explanation: the FFN, the shortcuts and the other blocks also decide.

§11 · Worked example

The attention of 3 tokens with , by hand

The same numbers as the chart of idea 2 in the simple version.

The setup. A trip of only 3 tokens: “departure”, “Madrid” and “return”. Each token has an embedding of 2 numbers. We want to know what mix “return” takes with one attention head: how much weight it puts on each token and what vector comes out.

Example map

We get the query of “return” and the keys and values of the three tokens, score each token with a dot product, divide by √2, turn the scores into weights with softmax and mix the values. At the end we see what changes without dividing and what the mask does on the row of “Madrid”.

  1. The constants: where each number comes from.
  2. Query, keys and values.
  3. The scores: three dot products.
  4. Scaling: dividing by √2.
  5. Softmax: from scores to weights.
  6. The mix of the values.
  7. Without scaling and with the mask.

  1. The constants: where each number comes from

    In words

    Each token comes in as its embedding (topic 10), here with only 2 numbers so it can be drawn. The three matrices of the attention head are learned in a real model; here we pick them with round numbers so the math can be followed by hand. and are the identity: they leave the embedding as it is.

    The math

    symbolvaluewhat it is
    2 numbersthe embedding of token (plus its position, which we leave out here). No units
    2 × 2the matrix that turns an embedding into a query: “what I'm looking for”
    2 × 2the one that turns it into a key: “what I am”
    2 × 2the one that turns it into a value: “what I give if someone looks at me”
    2how many numbers each query and each key has; its square root is the scale factor of §3

    What it means: the head has 3 matrices of 2 × 2, 12 numbers. In the model of §6, each head has 3 matrices of 16 × 8.

  2. Query, keys and values

    In words

    Each row is multiplied by the matrix (math topic 3): each number of the output is the sum of the row's numbers times one column of the matrix. “return” asks, so we need its query and the keys and values of all of them.

    The math

    What it means: the query of “return” points up and a bit to the left: toward the key of “Madrid”, far from the one of “departure”.

  3. The scores: three dot products

    In words

    The dot product multiplies number by number and adds up (math topic 2). It's high if the two arrows point the same way.

    The math

    Why does “return” score itself?

    Because with the causal mask each token sees the earlier ones and itself. “return” is the last of the three, so the mask hides nothing from it.

    What it means: “Madrid” matches best (2), then “return” (1), and “departure” doesn't match at all (−1).

  4. Scaling: dividing by √2

    In words

    Each score is divided by the square root of the number of components, , so that its size doesn't depend on how many numbers each arrow has (§3).

    The math

    Where does the 1.41421 come from?

    It's : the number that multiplied by itself gives 2. With 64 components per head, as in the base Transformer, you would divide by .

    What it means: the differences between scores shrink: from 3 to 2.12 between “Madrid” and “departure”.

  5. Softmax: from scores to weights

    In words

    The softmax (topic 4) raises to each score, so everything is positive, and divides by the sum, so the weights add up to 1.

    The math

    Why and not something else?

    Any positive, increasing function would give weights, but with the gradient of the softmax is very simple (topic 4), and adding a constant to all the scores changes nothing: that's why the code subtracts the maximum before exponentiating.

    What it means: “return” pays 62.0% of its attention to “Madrid”, 30.6% to itself and 7.4% to “departure”. They add up to 100%.

  6. The mix of the values

    In words

    The output of “return” is the sum of the values, each one multiplied by its weight.

    The math

    What is done next with ?

    In a block, it's multiplied by and added to the embedding of “return” through the shortcut (§5). What “return” took from “Madrid” stays in its numbers that way, and the final layer can predict “Madrid” as the next token.

    What it means: the output is much closer to the value of “Madrid”, , than to that of “departure”, .

  7. Without scaling and with the mask

    In words

    Two checks. Without dividing by √2, the softmax gets −1, 2 and 1 as they are. And the row of “Madrid”, token 2: with the causal mask, it can't look at “return”, which comes after it.

    The math

    Where does the 2.12132 come from?

    It's the difference between the two visible scores, . With two candidates, the softmax depends only on that difference: we divide top and bottom by . And : “return” gets weight 0.

    What it means: without scaling, “Madrid” goes from 62.0% to 70.5%: with only 2 components the effect is small; with 64, as in §3, it would be all or nothing. And the mask spreads all of “Madrid”'s weight over what has already happened. ejemplo.py reproduces these numbers and the row of “return” from F.scaled_dot_product_attention with is_causal=True.

ejemplo.py · reproduces the numbers above and checks them with PyTorch

"""The worked example: the attention of "return" over a 3-token trip with d = 2, by hand, and checked with
F.scaled_dot_product_attention."""
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

fichas = ["departure", "Madrid", "return"]
X = np.array([[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]])            # their embeddings (one row per token)
Wq = np.array([[1.0, 1.0], [-2.0, 1.0]]); Wk = np.eye(2); Wv = np.eye(2)
Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
print("q of return:", Q[2], "· keys k:", K.tolist())
s = K @ Q[2]                                                   # q·k with each token
print("scores q·k:", s, "· ÷√2:", np.round(s / np.sqrt(2), 5))
e = np.exp(s / np.sqrt(2))
w = e / e.sum()
print("e^(q·k/√2):", np.round(e, 5), "· sum", round(e.sum(), 5))
print("weights:", np.round(w, 5), "· sum to", w.sum())
o = w @ V
print("output = sum of weights × v:", np.round(o, 5))
e1 = np.exp(s); print("without dividing by √2, weights:", np.round(e1 / e1.sum(), 5))
m = np.exp(K[:2] @ Q[1] / np.sqrt(2)); print("row of Madrid with causal mask (only departure and Madrid):",
                                            "q =", Q[1], "weights", np.round(m / m.sum(), 5))
t = torch.tensor
ref = F.scaled_dot_product_attention(t(Q)[None], t(K)[None], t(V)[None], is_causal=True)[0]
print("PyTorch, row of return:", np.round(ref[2].numpy(), 5), "· error", float(np.abs(ref[2].numpy() - o).max()))

actual output

# q of return: [-1.  2.] · keys k: [[1.0, 0.0], [0.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]]
# scores q·k: [-1.  2.  1.] · ÷√2: [-0.70711  1.41421  0.70711]
# e^(q·k/√2): [0.49307 4.11325 2.02811] · sum 6.63443
# weights: [0.07432 0.61999 0.3057 ] · sum to 1.0
# output = sum of weights × v: [0.38001 0.92568]
# without dividing by √2, weights: [0.03512 0.70538 0.2595 ]
# row of Madrid with causal mask (only departure and Madrid): q = [-2.  1.] weights [0.10704 0.89296]
# PyTorch, row of return: [0.38001 0.92568] · error 5.551115123125783e-17

What would change in a real system

  • Learned matrices, not chosen by hand, and with 64 or 128 columns per head.
  • Many heads and blocks: the output of this step goes through , the shortcut, the norm and the FFN, and enters the next block.
  • The position added to each embedding before computing , and .
  • Long sequences: thousands of tokens, with the weight matrix computed in blocks.
